title: The Gold Mines in Supply Chains
summary: A reminder that huge wealth often hides in the supply chain behind everyday products.

blocks.alt: Convocation gowns image from the original post
blocks.caption: our goated convocation picture in the central lawns of BITS Goa

blocks.value: Last week, I went to my alma mater one last time as a student for my convocation. A very clean and ironed satin gown, scarf, and cap made up the attire of the 1,000 students who received their degrees with pride. We had to pay a refundable security deposit of INR 1,000/$12.5 to receive the attire, and we returned it to the admin after the ceremony to claim our deposit.

You take hundreds of lifetime pictures in that attire with people with whom you have spent about 20% of your life up to that point. But what do you do with a satin gown that is useless once the day is over? You probably never wear it again and let it rot in some corner of your attic. Or you return it to the admin and get your money back, unless you want to keep it as a souvenir.
But where did these hundreds of gowns come from?
The admin might have bought them long ago and recycled the same gowns every year. That could be one option, but it involves a lot of space for inventory and significant effort for maintenance.
Or, the admin could have rented them out for the day from some vendor.

Apparently, I learned that there are only two big rental vendors for satin gowns in all of India (or probably the entire subcontinent). They handle maintenance and rent thousands of gowns to thousands of colleges (like ours) across the subcontinent every year. Thinking about the scale, if you look at India, approximately 65 lakh graduates pass out every year, according to The Hans India. That is a huge market.

You know what is more interesting? The market and tradition for satin gowns have existed since the colonial era, and the same vendor who provided gowns for us also provided a gown to Smt. Indira Gandhi, the former Prime Minister of India, 50 years ago.

Everything we use every day has a deep supply chain and a gold mine waiting to be discovered if we look closely. Look at things around you and trace them back to the source, and you will surprise yourself with what you discover. Ball bearings are present in almost every rotating part around you, such as fans and cars. Those bearings might have been manufactured by SKF India. Incense sticks are made from incense powder, and only a handful of companies manufacture it.
You don't have to build for the next big thing to create wealth. There is wealth that can be created in the supply chain of the next big thing. And there is plenty of gold to be mined. Anywhere.
